signals.title: TASTESLOP

Argues genuine taste requires social validation and esoteric knowledge AI cannot replicate, and that tech's obsession with taste is anxiety about whether economic capital can capture cultural capital.

Engages computer vision and generative AI as forces reshaping how reality is perceived and trusted.

signals.title: Everything's probably fake now

Cites a Rwandan creator (@whotfisrw) and the stark math — ~$1M/month buys 600M views across 35,000 videos vs. a UK journalist earning £140 for 1.5M TikTok views.

signals.title: The bubble is getting a lot bubblier, folks

Suggests that if giants cannibalize core products chasing unprofitable AI, the broader internet could end up healthier and less Google/Meta-dependent.

signals.title: An internet after search engines

signals.title: Music Gives New Meaning to Josh Johnson's Comedy in His HBO Special 'Symphony'
signals.summary: Craft interview with Josh Johnson on integrating a live musical score into his HBO stand-up special, examining how orchestration reframes comedic timing and meaning.

signals.title: What a Spider Can Teach Cinematographers About Film Noir
signals.summary: Cinematography essay using Spider-Noir to interrogate the visual grammar of film noir, connecting contemporary genre work to classic noir lighting and shadow conventions.

signals.title: How to Make a Soundtrack Album for a TV Show
signals.summary: Craft feature on assembling a TV soundtrack album (Nobody Wants This S2), detailing music supervision choices and how album curation extends a show's identity.

signals.title: 'Lord of the Flies' Channels the Magic of Trees — and Also 'Lone Survivor'
signals.summary: Making-of interview with Jack Thorne on the Netflix Lord of the Flies adaptation, discussing location craft and survival-film influences shaping the production's naturalism.

signals.title: Meme Culture's Corrosive Effect on the American Heart
signals.summary: Alyssa Charpentier argues memes function as thought-terminating clichés that dehumanize people across the political spectrum, warning that celebrating tragedy through humor echoes historical patterns of dehumanization preceding authoritarianism.

signals.title: Why Tokyo Has So Many Record Stores
signals.summary: Essay examining how Tokyo sustains roughly 250 record stores while Western cities lost theirs, attributing survival to aggressive store differentiation, rail-driven walkable neighborhoods, and a collector culture treating physical media as cultural objects.

signals.title: Did Drake and Kendrick Lamar Kill Battle Rap?
signals.summary: Cultural criticism interrogating whether the commercialized, chart-driven Drake–Kendrick feud hollowed out the competitive spirit and craft of traditional battle rap.

signals.title: 'Recomposed' Performs a Fundamental Interpretation of the Music Industry
signals.summary: Books essay on Kyle Devine's work, reframing the music industry through an ecological lens that foregrounds the material and environmental costs of recorded-music formats.

signals.title: Vampires and the Ecstasy of Consumer Submission
signals.summary: Cross-medium essay reading the vampire figure as an allegory for consumer capitalism, analyzing the genre's eroticization of submission and consumption.

signals.title: Teo Hernández's Queer Avant-Garde Films Rewire Your Brain
signals.summary: Film essay on experimental filmmaker Teo Hernández, examining how his queer avant-garde aesthetics challenge perceptual norms and conventional narrative cinema.

signals.title: We've Got A File On You: Radiohead's Ed O'Brien
signals.summary: Career-spanning interview with O'Brien on his solo album Blue Morpho, born from pandemic depression and childhood trauma, his 432 Hz tuning philosophy, and his work beyond Radiohead including 7 Worlds Collide.

signals.title: "It's Strange To Be Talking About the Flaming Lips In The Past Tense": An Interview With Steven Drozd
signals.summary: Reflective Q&A with Drozd discussing the apparent winding-down of the Flaming Lips and his perspective on the band's legacy, framed as an elegiac look back at a defining career.

signals.title: The Story Behind Every Song On Kevin Morby's Masterful New Album Little Wide Open
signals.summary: Track-by-track Footnotes interview in which Morby annotates the songwriting and biographical context behind Little Wide Open, giving a granular look at his compositional process.

signals.title: Kim Petras Takes A Detour Off The Pop Highway
signals.summary: Interview/feature on Kim Petras pivoting away from mainstream pop conventions, examining the artistic and commercial stakes of her stylistic detour.

signals.title: We've Got A File On You: Broken Social Scene's Kevin Drew
signals.summary: Career-retrospective interview with Drew covering Broken Social Scene's collective ethos and his role in the 2000s indie-rock landscape.

signals.title: Low Culture Essay: Mary Chiney on Stanley Okorie's Nollywood Soundtracks
signals.summary: Essay arguing early Nollywood's true avant-garde lived in its soundtracks, with composer Stanley Okorie writing hyper-specific synth-pop that narrated film plots; Chiney warns that streaming algorithms demanding 'chill vibes' from African music threaten these works' survival.

signals.title: Rotting Tape and the Gentrification of African Pop: Why We Must Save the Nollywood Archive
signals.summary: Black Sky Thinking essay on the physical decay of Nollywood film and music archives, framing preservation as a fight against the gentrification and Western repackaging of African pop heritage.

signals.title: Low Culture Essay: James Bailey on The Driver's Seat by Muriel Spark
signals.summary: Literary-cultural essay reading Muriel Spark's The Driver's Seat as a low-culture touchstone, drawing out its unsettling treatment of agency and female narrative control.

signals.title: Combustible Material: Siouxsie and the Banshees' Tinderbox at 40
signals.summary: Anniversary essay reassessing Siouxsie and the Banshees' Tinderbox four decades on, situating the album within post-punk's evolution and the band's shifting cultural standing.

signals.title: This Year's Most Anticipated Horror Movie Captures One of the Internet's Eeriest Phenomena
signals.summary: Cultural analysis of the Backrooms film tracing its origins in 4chan creepypasta and explaining how internet-native liminal-space dread translates to mainstream horror cinema.

signals.title: Stanford Was Once a Cradle of Innovation. What It's Turned Into Is Something Else Entirely.
signals.summary: Essay (via Theo Baker's book) arguing Stanford has shifted from an innovation hub to a feeder for Silicon Valley VC power, critiquing the university's entanglement with tech wealth.

signals.title: Cannes Tried to Ban Nudity. Celebrities Revolted—and an Iconic Fashion Tradition Was Born.
signals.summary: Fashion-culture feature on Cannes 2026's nudity ban and the celebrity pushback, tracing how red-carpet defiance crystallized into an enduring festival fashion tradition.

signals.title: TV's Best Comedy Went Out With a Perfect Finale. It Was Years in the Making.
signals.summary: Showrunner interview/analysis of the Hacks finale, examining how Aniello and Statsky engineered the series' long-arc payoff and its place in modern TV comedy.

signals.title: He Was Supposed to Be "Canceled." He Just Broke One of Michael Jackson's Most Enduring Records.
signals.summary: Music-culture essay on Drake's chart resurgence post-Kendrick feud, interrogating what 'cancellation' means commercially when an artist still breaks Michael Jackson's Billboard records.

signals.title: Internet Is Celebrating the Fictional Villains Who Commit Atrocities but Are Somehow More Progressive Than the Heroes
signals.summary: Roundup of an online discourse trend in which users praise fictional villains as more ideologically progressive than the heroes; touches on fan-politics reading but stays largely at the tweet-aggregation level rather than sustained analysis.

signals.title: field notes from a phone-free future
signals.summary: Aleksic reports on an emerging countercultural movement rejecting smartphone dependency and algorithmic optimization in favor of unmediated, subjective experience. Frames it as 'representation against representation' - a refusal to let corporate platforms categorize and commodify lived experience.

signals.title: the monsters hiding in your algorithm
signals.summary: Argues that beneath TikTok's curated algorithmic surface lies an incomprehensible 'terra incognita' of absurdist, nonsensical content. Positions these online 'monsters' as modern mythology - warnings about the unknowable vastness beneath our ordered digital world, like ancient mythical creatures explaining the inexplicable.

signals.title: you don't know where anything comes from
signals.summary: Contends that consumers are willfully ignorant of the origins of products, ideas, and memes they consume, making them 'civically negligent' and diminishing lived experience. Argues that actively questioning sources - of wool sweaters, avocados, or viral memes alike - is what yields genuine satisfaction and better citizenship.

signals.title: moloch and the machines
signals.summary: Frames modern society as Moloch, sacrificing human connection for algorithmic optimization, and proposes real-world community events as the antidote - demonstrated via a public reading of Ginsberg's 'Howl' in Washington Square Park. Explores the paradox of using social media to critique social media, concluding 'the event is the medium.'

signals.title: how to look at brainrot
signals.summary: Argues that AI-generated 'brainrot' memes deserve serious artistic consideration as contemporary folk art with genuine emotional and psychological effects. Advocates analyzing memes through phenomenology and context rather than dismissing them, since they 'resonate with other human beings.'

signals.title: symbiotic virality
signals.summary: Distinguishes 'parasitic virality' (one-sided extraction treating people as means) from 'mutualistic virality' (mutual benefit), arguing that social media virality often exploits people. Contends meaningful online communication requires prioritizing community-building over content creation for its own sake.

signals.title: 'The Drama' and the microgenerational digital divide
signals.summary: Uses the film 'The Drama' to argue the Zoomer-Millennial divide hinges on whether one's adolescent transgressions were digitally documented. Millennials' youthful mistakes went unrecorded, while Zoomers face permanently archived pasts, producing divergent attitudes toward guilt, accountability, and forgiveness.

signals.title: People prefer A.I. art because people prefer bad art
signals.summary: Argues people favor AI-generated art not for superior creativity but because they prefer accessible, straightforward kitsch over challenging human work. Critiques Scott Alexander's AI Art Turing Test as designed to obscure distinguishing features, citing a Nature study where AI poems outscored Eliot and Shakespeare for being more 'straightforward.'

signals.title: Who Is Nick Bilton?
signals.summary: A sustained critical profile arguing that tech columnist Nick Bilton - reportedly being installed by Bari Weiss to lead 60 Minutes - is unqualified, a 'hatchet man' positioned to further degrade the news organization. Constructs a unified thesis about Bilton's career across the NYT, Vanity Fair, and TV rather than a link roundup.

signals.title: Sexless Little Carnivores
signals.summary: Emily Kenway traces the cultural history of pet food, from Victorian fears that fresh meat caused canine 'nymphomania' to today's premium 'ancestral'-diet brands. Argues these brands sell the fantasy of a pet's wildness while delivering fully domesticated predators eating from pouches, a proxy for evolving human-animal control.

signals.title: Eight People, One Hob
signals.summary: Nell Whittaker critiques the social-media romanticization of communal house-share cooking, arguing shared kitchens usually stem from financial necessity, not commune ideology. Includes a practical 'recipe' for cooking five distinct meals on a single stovetop as a portrait of the unaesthetic mundanity of cohabitation.

signals.title: The Rise and Fall of Mercato Metropolitano
signals.summary: Caterina Urbano examines how one London street-food market embodied the contradictions of urban regeneration, foodie consumerism, and place-making. Uses the market's trajectory as a lens on gentrification and the commodification of conviviality.

signals.title: Your Machine is Killing You
signals.summary: Fenja Akinde-Hummel explores microwave conspiracy theories and the domestic anxieties around appliance technology, particularly as they circulate within families. Treats kitchen-tech fear as a window onto distrust of modernity and the gendered politics of the home.

signals.title: There's injustice in Palestine that needs to be repaired, that's the priority
signals.summary: Interview with chef Fadi Kattan and Sara Asad-Mannings on running Palestinian food businesses in London, situating cuisine within questions of justice, displacement, and cultural repair. Food becomes a vehicle for political and diasporic claims.

signals.title: Edward Skeletrix: The Mind as Masterpiece
signals.summary: Cassidy George profiles multimedia artist Edward Skeletrix (Edward King Bass IV) over absinthe in London, covering his music/photography/performance practice and his recovery from mental-health struggles via spiritual teaching. He deliberately makes unsettling work to interrogate viewers' conditioned bodily responses to stimuli.

signals.title: Ultrace: 'A car is an object of applied art'
signals.summary: Julia Kraeplin interviews Adrian Kapica, founder of Polish automotive collective Ultrace, on reframing car culture as fine art and sculpture. Covers the collective's first international event, 'Archived Dreams,' in Düsseldorf in April 2026.

signals.title: The Internet is Air with Maya Man
signals.summary: Em Mai Chmiel interviews artist Maya Man on internet culture, self-curation as embodied performance, and her skepticism toward fashionable neo-Luddism. Draws on Man's background as a competition dancer and her StarQuest/StarPower project staging the aestheticized self, ahead of her bitforms solo show opening March 19, 2026.

signals.title: A conversation with Dea Kulumbegashvili for Apartamento magazine issue #36
signals.summary: An interview-as-portrait with Georgian filmmaker Dea Kulumbegashvili, photographed between Berlin and Eastern Georgia, in Apartamento's signature register of how a cultural figure actually lives and inhabits domestic space. Ties her interior life and surroundings to her filmmaking.

signals.title: A conversation with Mijae Kim
signals.summary: A Seoul-set conversation/home portrait of Mijae Kim, part of Apartamento's domestic-life-as-cultural-signal approach, with photography by Hasisi Park. Examines the subject's living environment as a window onto personal and creative identity.

signals.title: The Last Cow
signals.summary: Sarah Thankam Mathews contributes a dystopian fiction piece on longing for something one has never had, using scarcity of dairy/sweetness as its central image. Treats the cultural and bodily weight of craving in a depleted future. (NOTE: cakezine.org domain is compromised; editorial now lives at cakezine.substack.com.)

signals.title: Was It Worth It?
signals.summary: Adam Dalva connects Ozempic, grief, and the 'theater of all-you-can-eat dining,' interrogating appetite, indulgence, and the body in an era of pharmaceutical hunger-suppression. Sweetness and excess become a lens on contemporary anxieties about desire.

signals.title: What A Mess
signals.summary: A conversation with chef Brooks Headley on running a lacto-vegetarian restaurant (Superiority Burger) in carnivorous NYC, treating dessert and meatless cooking as cultural provocation. Frames the restaurant as a ritual space negotiating pleasure and ethics.

signals.title: The Invention of Summer
signals.summary: Xita Rubert explores loneliness, grief, and the ways we recognize pieces of ourselves in strangers, framed through seasonal sweetness and memory. Sensory food cues anchor a meditation on connection and loss.

signals.title: Architecture in the 21st Century
signals.summary: Kate Wagner argues architecture accelerated over 25 years from Deconstructivism through Parametricism to 'blobitecture,' driven by digital tools and social media that deskilled the profession while minting celebrity starchitects. Calls for the discipline to confront power, surveillance, and inequality rather than retreat into stylistic nostalgia. (NOTE: PIN-UP articles live at pinupmagazine.org/articles, not pinuphome.com.)

signals.title: Dozie Kanu's First Foray into Mass-Production
signals.summary: Victoria Camblin interviews artist-designer Dozie Kanu on his move from collectible design to fine art and his 2026 Knoll collaboration, framed by his relocation to Portugal and his Nigerian-Texan heritage. Kanu describes using familiar objects as a 'conceptual luring mechanism' to surface histories of colonialism and Black representation.

signals.title: Notes Towards Biotic Architecture (We the Bacteria)
signals.summary: A Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley piece (with Josh Daube) on biotic, microbial framings of architecture, reconceiving buildings and bodies as colonized by and continuous with bacterial life. Pushes design discourse toward the entanglement of the built environment and the body's biome.

signals.title: Frank Gehry Reflects on His Legacy
signals.summary: An interview in which Frank Gehry looks back on his career and legacy for PIN-UP's 20th-anniversary Issue 40. Reflects on the trajectory of his work and its place in contemporary architectural culture.

signals.title: Into the Right-Wing Dreamworld
signals.summary: Mitch Therieau argues the second Trump administration governs through propagandistic imagery rather than rhetoric, fusing fascist iconography, frontier mythology, and state violence into emotionally resonant 'dream logic' symbols (e.g. a viral penguin video). The visual regime expresses an annihilationist impulse: a wounded desire to restore an imagined past by destroying whatever blocks it.

signals.title: Directing the Herd
signals.summary: Edward Ongweso Jr. revisits the Lippmann-Dewey debate over whether masses can self-govern, arguing that corporate digital platforms have replaced genuine public discourse with algorithmic management. The result is competing fragmented sub-publics rather than collective deliberation, with AI now threatening what remains of democratic knowledge-sharing.

signals.title: History Has Its Eyes on You: Slam Frank and Musical Theater's Hamilton Bind
signals.summary: Emma Adler examines how Hamilton and its imitators tried to reconcile history with progressive values, and why that formula now reads as flawed—dramatizing historical suffering alongside modern grievance paradoxically trivializes present concerns. She argues satirical works like Slam Frank and Oh, Mary! better capture audience disillusionment by abandoning the pretense that progressive retelling can be gotten 'right.'

signals.title: R is for Relation
signals.summary: Emily Eyestone reviews the exhibition 'The Earth, the Fire, the Water, and the Winds: For a Museum of Errantry with Édouard Glissant,' tracing how Glissant's concepts of relation and archipelagic thinking materialize in visual art. She focuses on his collaboration with sculptor Agustín Cárdenas, whose work eke out a beginning from barren landscapes—embodying Glissant's vision of making meaning from historical trauma and ecological devastation.

signals.title: Marked Down
signals.summary: Nicole Lipman reads the Sex and the City sequel through its costuming, arguing Molly Rogers' designs lack the narrative integration that made Patricia Field's originals iconic. The piece contends the film uses glamour to mask uncomfortable truths about media-industry collapse, offering laid-off journalists a fantasy of quick reemployment rather than genuine critique of precarity.

signals.title: Not Quite Nonsense
signals.summary: Mae Losasso reviews Jennifer Scappettone's Poetry After Barbarism, which frames xenoglossic poetry (writing in 'tongues officially foreign' to the poet) as resistance to fascism and nationalism through linguistic instability. Losasso argues that while Scappettone's call for 'studious unlearning' opens real political possibilities, it risks obscuring the substantial expertise such poetic practice actually demands.

signals.title: The Loneliness of the Competitive Quizzer
signals.summary: Drew Basile argues competitive quizzing offers isolated, often unemployed knowledge workers a pseudo-meritocratic refuge where fact accumulation supplies identity and purpose. Yet the system reinforces the loneliness it promises to cure, an endless arms race masking anxieties about labor-market obsolescence and the futility of knowledge 'the market certainly wouldn't reward.'

signals.title: Boy Girl Problems
signals.summary: Grace Byron argues Katherine Packert Burke's novel All Us Saints subverts the 'trans killer' trope by revealing the murderer upfront and forcing readers to confront the transphobia and trauma that shaped him rather than sensationalizing the violence. The review interrogates how true-crime narrative and cultural mythology obscure complex crimes while holding audiences accountable for their fascination with violent spectacle.

signals.title: Superhuman Fantasies
signals.summary: Nicholas Low argues Silicon Valley techno-optimists like Marc Andreessen misappropriate Nietzsche's Übermensch by equating superhuman transcendence with technological enhancement and computational speed. Nietzsche, Low contends, envisioned the superhuman as one who affirms finitude and suffering rather than escaping it through technology—so genuine self-overcoming requires renouncing the nihilistic urge to engineer suffering away.

signals.title: Why creativity shines out on the edge of things
signals.summary: The essay argues that creativity—biological and cultural—flourishes at edges: the margins of a population, the rim of a landmass, the boundary of viability or orthodoxy. Drawing on island ecology (field mice on St Kilda) and Iain McGilchrist, it treats 'edges' as metaphor and material fact, claiming that fecundity arises precisely where old inhibitions relax and new challenges press.

signals.title: How does the deep Earth see humanity?
signals.summary: The essay argues that from the planet's perspective humans are a 'shallow' species, yet our subsurface influence is now staggering—human-caused fluid flux from oil, gas, and mining exceeds natural deep groundwater flow below 500 metres. It reframes the Anthropocene debate around how deep human influence reaches (into the upper mantle, the carbon shift from lithosphere to atmosphere) rather than merely when it began.

signals.title: Why we need to think again about ecosystem failure
signals.summary: Written by a philosopher-ecologist, the essay argues that calling an ecosystem 'failed' (an algal bloom, coral bleaching) imports human duties, norms, and objectives that are external to the ecosystem itself. It bridges philosophical debates over the concept of 'function' with ecologists' unreflective use of the same word, questioning whether ecosystems can fail in any sense independent of human concern.

signals.title: Kony 2012 Forever
signals.summary: Andrew Lee argues Kony 2012 pioneered a propaganda model that stripped political complexity from Uganda's conflict—obscuring Western-backed government abuses while casting the LRA as pure evil requiring military intervention. He contends this template of decontextualized atrocity footage, built to manufacture demand for military action, has become a blueprint shaping how Western audiences consume later conflicts.

signals.title: Will gossip save digital media?
signals.summary: As Google's AI search guts SEO-driven traffic, Kate Lindsay argues digital media must pivot to content AI can't replicate. She suggests gossip and personality-driven journalism may become the differentiator that keeps outlets alive in the post-search landscape.

signals.title: I let Apple AI answer all my texts
signals.summary: Lindsay documents an experiment using Apple's AI-suggested replies to fix her habit of leaving texts unanswered. The feature instead produced vague, sometimes rude messages that alienated her contacts—an essay on how automating intimacy degrades rather than smooths human connection.

signals.title: The social contract around phones is broken
signals.summary: Using Alamo Drafthouse's move to phone-based ordering during films as a case, Lindsay argues phone etiquette's shared social contract has collapsed. People increasingly treat others as 'NPCs' and public spaces as extensions of their personal digital worlds rather than shared rooms requiring mutual consideration.

signals.title: We don't deserve the personal essay boom
signals.summary: Lindsay argues internet culture has grown too morally serious and outrage-driven to enjoy the personal essay revival, turning innocent annoyances into accusations and attacking essay subjects rather than appreciating the writing. (Republished in-window; flagged as a repost of a 2024 essay.)

signals.title: Chartbook 450: Modern growth surges. Or, why China's economic development is unique in human history
signals.summary: Tooze argues China's 1978-2022 growth is the largest single transformation in world economic history, distinct in both scale and velocity from prior industrializations. He marshals coal-consumption and GDP-growth comparisons across earlier expansions to show why the conventional catch-up framing understates how anomalous China's surge is.

signals.title: Unemployment and burnout issues spotlighted by Arts University Plymouth students
signals.summary: Dezeen School Shows feature on Arts University Plymouth graduate work, including a graphic/communication project about entering the creative industries amid self-employment, economic uncertainty and AI-generated imagery, plus a toolkit for creatives experiencing burnout. Frames precarity and AI anxiety as the defining conditions for emerging designers.

signals.title: Time management pebble among industrial design projects from the University of Illinois Chicago
signals.summary: UIC industrial design students present assistive objects for neurodivergent people, led by 'Pebs' — a system of small glowing objects supporting awareness of time, task initiation and transitions for people who struggle with time perception and sustained focus. Signals a shift toward neurodivergence-centered, calm-tech product design.

signals.title: Flood-management infrastructure among projects from the School of Visual Arts
signals.summary: SVA student work including 'ReLoop,' a public food-rescue hub that intercepts surplus and cosmetically imperfect produce from farmers and redirects it to food-insecure communities while making the logistics visible. Emphasis on civic infrastructure and making invisible systems legible.

signals.title: Centre for dance and wellbeing among projects from IE University
signals.summary: IE University project 'El Ritmo de Casa Común' reimagines luxury as a shared condition inside Nave 15 at Matadero Madrid, organizing a three-level domestic system (thermal pools and kitchen, wooden rehearsal platforms, insulated housing) where circulation turns movement into spatial choreography. Reframes luxury from individual consumption to communal access supporting bodily practice.

signals.title: Arching motion-informed amphitheatre among projects from University of Dundee
signals.summary: University of Dundee project 'Cambré' reimagines the amphitheatre as a grid of differently shaped arches over a sunken stage in Dundee Botanic Gardens, with form derived from dance and motion. Part of a society-driven student cohort applying choreographic logic to public architecture.

signals.title: Proposal for sustainable agriculture factory among projects from UWE Bristol
signals.summary: MArch student Danni Payne (tutors Matthew Hynam, Piers Taylor, Michael Lewis) proposes a 2050 agriculture factory built from shaggy thatch, exposed timber and manure plaster, returning industrial production to the high street with soil-research labs and exhibition galleries above. Argues for an 'honest,' materially-expressive approach to re-localized agriculture.

signals.title: Zero-waste textiles project among work featured at New Designers 2026
signals.summary: New Designers 2026 preview led by 'Interwoven: Reclaiming the Domestic Fibre,' a textiles project using found, deadstock and second-hand yarn via a zero-waste construction process of laser-cutting and reassembling knitted panels. Continues the material-circularity and domestic-craft revival thread among UK graduates.

signals.title: Homeware objects that support ADHD individuals among work at New Designers 2026
signals.summary: New Designers 2026 feature on homeware objects designed to support people with ADHD in daily domestic routines. Reinforces a 2026 grad-cohort pattern of neurodivergence-informed product and homeware design.

signals.title: Rehab centre among projects from Florence Institute of Design International
signals.summary: Florence Institute of Design International interior design students present work led by a rehabilitation centre for young people struggling with addiction. Signals interior-design students addressing youth mental health and recovery environments.

signals.title: Proposal for beer factory museum among projects from the University of Bath
signals.summary: University of Bath architecture students present work led by a proposal for a beer factory museum, part of a broader cohort interest in productive/industrial heritage buildings as cultural and public destinations.

signals.title: Sculptural wooden play apparatus among projects from the Architectural Association
signals.summary: AA School (London) student work led by a sculptural timber play apparatus, shown ahead of the school's end-of-year Projects Review. Reflects a play/childhood-spatial-experience strand in 2026 architecture grad work.

signals.title: Ecological research centre with tree-inspired design among projects from Politecnico di Torino and University of Belgrade
signals.summary: Joint Politecnico di Torino / University of Belgrade architecture projects led by an ecological research centre whose form is informed by the 'growth rings' of trees; the showcase also includes a science museum with a timber thatched roof and a school extension with library and playground. Biomorphic and timber-forward ecological architecture from emerging students.

signals.title: Ten young designers and studios to watch from Salone Satellite 2026
signals.summary: Roundup of ten emerging designers and recently-graduated studios spotlighted at Salone Satellite 2026 in Milan, the under-35 emerging-designer platform within Salone del Mobile. Useful early-career practitioner signal adjacent to grad-show season.

signals.title: Miggie Bacungan's graphic design challenges the artificial flavouring of pop culture imagery
signals.summary: Discover/Ones-to-Watch profile of Miggie Bacungan, a Parañaque (Philippines) visual-communication student and freelance designer who builds 'organised chaos' from Manila street markets, tarpaulin ads and bootleg imagery. Project 'Kain Tayo' critiques economic inequality by depicting people resorting to eating inedible objects amid inhumane food costs, exposing poverty beneath hyper-saturated consumer aesthetics.

signals.title: POV: Graphic design schools are teaching tech, but are they teaching taste?
signals.summary: Practitioner opinion piece by designer Kathy Pham arguing graphic-design education has become vocational, over-indexing on software skill ('Adobe wizards') at the expense of cultural literacy and critical thinking. Calls for treating graphic design as a liberal art to produce designers who can solve meaningful problems across contexts — a direct critique of current design-school pedagogy.

signals.title: Apply now for It's Nice That's Ones to Watch – championing the next generation of creatives
signals.summary: Launch of the 2026 Ones to Watch open call targeting creatives graduating, just-graduated, or with under a year in industry, across graphic design, illustration, photography, animation, art and short film. A leading-indicator signal for which emerging-talent disciplines and criteria the publication is foregrounding this cycle.

signals.title: New York Design Week Is Here, May 14–20
signals.summary: Core77's NY Design Week 2026 guide highlighting the 'Wanted' Schools Showcase at ICFF (Javits Center, May 17–19), which features student work from more than 20 design schools worldwide. Frames the schools showcase as a primary venue for emerging industrial/product design talent this season.

signals.title: RISD Grad Show 2026 to Open at the Rhode Island Convention Center on May 21
signals.summary: Announcement of RISD's 2026 Graduate Thesis Exhibition (May 21–30, Rhode Island Convention Center), presenting thesis work from 19 graduate programs — Architecture, Ceramics, Design Engineering, Digital+Media, Furniture, Glass, Graphic Design, Industrial Design, Jewelry+Metalsmithing, Textiles and more — in a custom 43,000-sf build. Each thesis represents one to three years of research and production; work also viewable digitally at risdgrad.show from May 21.
